question: Will H.R. 33 (United States–Taiwan Expedited Double-Tax Relief Act) be enacted into law before May 1, 2026?

causal-factors.name: Momentum from U.S.–Taiwan tax negotiations
causal-factors.rationale: The Treasury announced in Oct 2024 that the U.S. and Taiwan would begin negotiating a comprehensive tax agreement to address double taxation, which could unlock implementing legislation and broaden bipartisan support (source: U.S. Treasury press release).

causal-factors.name: House passage demonstrates broad bipartisan support
causal-factors.rationale: H.R. 33 passed the House in Jan 2025 by a 423–1 vote, signaling strong bipartisan backing that could help momentum in the Senate (source: Congress.gov All Info/House press releases; Ways & Means release).

causal-factors.name: Historical base rate for enactment of two-chamber bills
causal-factors.rationale: Historical analyses show a very small share of introduced federal bills become law, with bicameral passage and presidential signature remaining a substantial bottleneck (e.g., single-digit to low double-digit success rates across recent Congresses).

causal-factors.name: Election-year dynamics and legislative productivity headwinds
causal-factors.rationale: Midterm/election-year cycles typically depress legislative output and complicate passage of complex, bipartisan tax-relief legislation, consistent with observed low enactment rates in prior periods (sources discuss overall productivity trends in Congress).

causal-factors.name: Recent House passage and Senate companion introduced
causal-factors.rationale: The House passed H.R.33 423-1 (Jan 15, 2025) and a Senate companion was introduced soon after, signaling cross-chamber momentum (sources: turn0search3, turn0search7).

causal-factors.name: Senate status remains uncertain / no enacted status by 2026
causal-factors.rationale: As of March 1, 2026, there is no public record of Senate passage or presidential signature, indicating a stalled path despite House action (sources: turn0search1, turn0search7).

causal-factors.name: Ongoing momentum toward a U.S.–Taiwan tax agreement
causal-factors.rationale: Treasury highlighted negotiations for a comprehensive U.S.–Taiwan tax agreement in 2024, reflecting sustained momentum behind bilateral tax-relief efforts (source: turn0search0).

causal-factors.name: Bipartisan and bicameral nature of the effort
causal-factors.rationale: Public statements and press materials emphasize bipartisan and bicameral support for H.R. 33, suggesting potential for further movement in a divided Congress (sources: turn0search3, turn0search7).

causal-factors.name: Historical low passage rate for federal bills
causal-factors.rationale: Historical benchmarks show a very small share of introduced bills become law (often cited as well under 3%, with some analyses around 1%), implying a persistently low probability of enactment (sources: turn1search0, turn1search1).

causal-factors.name: Senate inaction after House passage
causal-factors.rationale: H.R. 33 passed the House on January 15, 2025 but there is no final Senate passage or presidential signature reported by May 1, 2026.

causal-factors.name: Senate companion bill introduced and bicameral momentum
causal-factors.rationale: A Senate companion bill to H.R. 33 was introduced on January 23, 2025, signaling ongoing bicameral attention and potential movement.

causal-factors.name: Ongoing US-Taiwan tax negotiations and potential broader tax treaty authority
causal-factors.rationale: Treasury announced in October 2024 that the U.S. and Taiwan would begin negotiations on a comprehensive tax agreement, and H.R. 33 would authorize a broader treaty framework.

causal-factors.name: Bipartisan advocacy and formal letters urging Senate action
causal-factors.rationale: June 2025 bipartisan letter urging prompt Senate consideration adds political pressure to move the bill forward.

causal-factors.name: Taiwan-related economic developments and cross-border investment commitments
causal-factors.rationale: Public signals of tax-related progress and cross-border investment context (e.g., 2025–2026 momentum around U.S.-Taiwan economic ties) provide a modest upward push.

causal-factors.name: Baseline historical enactment rate for such bills
causal-factors.rationale: Historical data show a very low share of introduced federal bills becoming law, constraining the odds even with forward momentum.

synthesis: The objections reveal real upside from Senate momentum and ongoing tax negotiations, but the historical bottlenecks for two-chamber federal legislation keep the outlook modest. Accordingly, the central estimate is nudged upward from 16% to about 20%, with a broad range reflecting substantial uncertainty.
